3.01.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this frame?"
- "An **external fixator**: pins in the bone, clamps, and rods outside the skin."
- "Name it by its frame: monolateral, ring, hybrid, hexapod or pelvic."

| Frame | Look for | Main use |
|---|---|---|
| **Monolateral, simple** | half pins, own clamps, straight rod | damage control, open fractures |
| **Monolateral, monotube** (rail) | thick telescoping body | lengthening, bone transport |
| **Ilizarov ring** | full rings, thin tensioned wires | lengthening, non-union, deformity |
| **Hybrid** | ring at joint, rod on shaft | tibial plateau, pilon |
| **Hexapod** | two rings, six oblique struts | complex deformity |
| **Pelvic** | iliac pins, anterior bar | unstable pelvic ring |

- Simple monolateral fixator on a bone model
- Monotube fixators on femur and tibia; rail for segment transport

### Classification (Handbook)
| Frame | Pins | Planes |
|---|---|---|
| **Unilateral uniplanar** | half pins | one |
| **Bilateral uniplanar** | full pins | one |
| Unilateral biplanar | half pins | two |
| Bilateral biplanar | full pins | two |
| **Circular** | complete rings | many |
| **Hybrid** | rings plus rods | many |

- Drawn frame types: laterality, planes, ring, hybrid

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Half pin, one side; full pin, both sides**

PITFALL — "is the bilateral frame still used?"
- AO calls the transfixing bilateral frame "now seldom used"
- Say → "**Rarely. The unilateral frame is the most common for fresh shaft fractures.**"

3.02.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what are the parts of this fixator?"
- "**Pins** hold the bone, **clamps** grip the pins, **rods** carry the load."
- "Pin size depends on the bone: always **under one third** of its width."

### Pins
- Schanz half pins and Steinmann or Denham full pins → ch 2
- Fixator pins range **3–6 mm**

| Bone (Handbook) | Pin |
|---|---|
| Femur | **6 mm** |
| Tibia | **5–6 mm** |
| Humerus | **5 mm** |
| Forearm | **4 mm** |
| Hand, foot | **3 mm** |

#### The one-third rule
- Pin diameter under **1/3** of the bone → no iatrogenic fracture
- A hole over **20–30%** of the bone raises fracture risk (Rockwood)
- In adults, **6 mm** is the largest safe pin

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Femur six, tibia five-six, humerus five, forearm four, hand three**

### Tips (AO; Rockwood)
| Tip | Feature | Best in |
|---|---|---|
| **Trocar** (standard) | needs predrilling always | diaphysis |
| **Self-tapping** | flutes cut the thread | predrilled hole |
| **Self-drilling** | drill-bit tip, one pass | metaphysis |

#### Self-drilling pins
- They grip about **25%** less bone than predrilled pins
- The tip may stick out **2–3 mm** past the far cortex

- Pin tips: short and long threads, HA self-drilling, titanium
- Thread designs: tapered, self-drilling, cancellous, cortical, HA-coated

### Metal and coating
- Pins are stainless steel or titanium
- **Hydroxyapatite (HA)** coating lets bone grow onto the pin
- Result: less loosening; chosen when the frame stays long

### Clamps
- **Single-pin** or **multi-pin** clamps
- Single-pin clamps let each pin point in any direction
- Clamp junctions are the weakest link → retighten during treatment

- Pin clamps on a model; AO clamp types

### Rods (AO)
| Rod | Feature |
|---|---|
| **Simple** | straight bar |
| **Hinged** (articulated) | crosses a joint, allows motion |
| **Telescoping** | slides: lengthening or shortening |

- Materials: stainless steel, titanium, aluminium, carbon fibre

| System | Rod |
|---|---|
| Large | **11 mm** |
| Medium | **8 mm** |
| Small | **4 mm** |
| Mini, for fingers | **2 mm** |

- Large rods take **4–6 mm** Schanz screws

- Steel tubes and carbon fibre rods

#### Hinged fixator
- Keeps a dislocated joint reduced and still lets it move
- Used most at the **elbow**

- Hinged elbow fixator, on the arm and on fluoroscopy

PITFALL — "an 8 mm pin in the tibia for more stiffness?"
- A hole over one third of the bone becomes a fracture line
- Say → "**No. Pin under one third of the bone; 6 mm is the adult maximum.**"

3.03.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this frame on the leg?"
- "A **monolateral fixator**: half pins from one side, clamps, one or two rods."
- "It gives **relative stability**, so the fracture heals by callus."

### Recognise it
- **Simple** (one clamp per pin) or **monotube** (telescoping body): see 3.1
- Monotube pin clusters are fixed at each end

### Indications (AO)
| Use | Example |
|---|---|
| **Damage control** | polytrauma, unstable patient |
| **Open fracture** | severe soft-tissue injury |
| **Joint spanning** | knee, ankle, wrist |
| **Infection** | infected fracture or non-union |
| Reduction tool | holds length during nailing |

- Handbook's preferred sites: anterior pelvic ring, pilon, comminuted distal radius
- Wrist frame: two pins in the second metacarpal, two in the radius

- Wrist-spanning fixator: metacarpal and radial pins

### Insertion (AO)
#### Plan
1) Pins outside the zone of injury and of future incisions
2) **Two pins** in each main fragment, spread wide apart
3) Stay out of the joint capsule → no joint sepsis

#### Insert (Campbell)
4) Stab incision in a safe zone; blunt dissection to bone
5) Trocar and drill sleeve centred on bone; sharp drill, slow, with pauses
6) Irrigate the sleeve with saline while drilling

- Trocar and drill sleeve on the bone

#### Finish
7) Insert the pin by hand; it grips the far cortex, not far beyond
8) Release tight skin around each pin
9) Rod close to the bone; tighten the clamps

### Safe corridors
| Site | Rule |
|---|---|
| Tibia | anteromedial face, not the crest |
| Arm, distal half | radial nerve at risk |
| Leg, third–fourth quarter junction | anterior tibial artery, deep peroneal nerve |

- The tibial crest is thick: it overheats and the drill slips
- Fluoroscopy halves the risk of nerve or vessel injury

- Safe zones for tibial pins

### Modular reduction
- Each fragment's pin pair goes on its own rod
- The pairs act as handles: reduce, then lock a third rod

- Pins placed, rods joined, reduction held

### Convert early (AO)
- Change to a nail or plate **within 2 weeks**: far fewer complications
- Pin sites older than **10–14 days** are taken as colonised
- Late change with dirty pins → a **"pin holiday"** of at least 10 days

- Femur spanned across the knee, then nailed at 12 days

PITFALL — "keep the frame six weeks, then nail?"
- The pin tracks colonise the canal; infection rises after two weeks
- Say → "**No. Convert within two weeks; later, give a pin holiday first.**"

3.04.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you make this frame more stable?"
- "**Reduce** the fracture first, then use **bigger, more, wider** pins."
- "Bring the rod **closer**, add a **second rod** and a **second plane**."

| Factor (Handbook; Nagah) | Stiffer when |
|---|---|
| **Reduction**, bone contact | most important |
| **Pin diameter** | larger: second most important |
| Pin number | 2 per fragment, 3 in femur |
| Pin spread | far apart in each fragment |
| Pin near fracture | close, outside the hematoma |
| Bone–rod distance | shorter |
| Rods | two, or stacked |
| Planes | multiplanar > biplanar > uniplanar |
| Pin coating | HA-coated |

- Stability factors: pin size, number, spread, bar, bone–pin interface

### The numbers (Rockwood)
- Bending stiffness rises with pin radius to the **fourth power**

| Pins compared | Bending stiffness |
|---|---|
| 6 mm vs 4 mm | about **5 times** |
| 6 mm vs 5 mm | **double** (AO) |

#### Pins
- Old, weak bone: use **three** pins each side, not two
- Pins in different planes: separated by more than **45°**

#### Steerage pins
- Half pins parallel to an oblique fracture turn shear into compression
- Shear appears beyond **30°** of obliquity
- Beyond **60°**, shear dominates

#### Carbon fibre bars
- About **15%** stiffer than steel tubes
- Yet the frame is only **85%** as stiff as with steel: clamps grip carbon less well

### Working length
- Distance between the innermost pins across the fracture
- Shorter working length → more stability

- Frame constructs in rising stiffness: single tube to bilateral
- Delta frame: drawing, and on a crushed tibia
- Double-stacked rods on a tibia

### Not too stiff
- A frame that is too rigid also delays union
- Later, weight bearing is the best way to dynamize
- Rigid definitive frames: delayed union in **20–30%** (Campbell)

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Reduce first; then fat, many, wide, near pins; a close, double rod; more planes**

PITFALL — "which factor matters most?"
- Pin size comes second; bone contact comes first
- Say → "**Reduction with bone contact; then pin diameter.**"

3.05.t: 3.5 Ilizarov Ring Fixator — The Full Card
3.05.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this ring frame?"
- "An **Ilizarov** frame: full rings, thin **tensioned wires**, connecting rods."
- "It allows weight bearing, lengthening, bone transport and deformity correction."

### Recognise it
- Rings around the limb; wires **1.5–2 mm** cross the bone
- **Olive wire**: a bead on the wire pushes the bone like a lag screw

- Ilizarov frames lengthening both tibiae, and their X-ray
- Ring frame on the tibia

### Parts and numbers
| Item (Miller; Nagah) | Number |
|---|---|
| Wire, adult | **1.8 mm** |
| Wire, child | **1.5 mm** |
| Wire tension | **90–130 kg** |
| Wire crossing angle | ideally **90°** |

- Each ring needs at least **two** wires or half pins
- One wire above the ring, one below → the ring does not bend

- Smooth and olive wires, tensioner, rings

### What makes it stiffer (Nagah; Rockwood; Campbell)
| Stiffer | Note |
|---|---|
| **Thicker wires**, more tension | most important |
| More wires, more rings | |
| Crossing angle near 90° | parallel wires let bone slide |
| **Olive wires** | stop sliding |
| **Smaller ring** | beats extra tension |
| Rings close to the fracture | |

- Axially it is only **25%** as stiff as a unilateral frame
- In bending and shear it equals pin fixators

- Wire crossing angles: 90°, 45–60°, nearly parallel
- Olive wires used as lag screws in a distal tibia

#### Keep the tension
- Bolt slippage is the main cause of lost tension
- Clamping a wire loses about **7%** of its tension
- Bolt torque over **20 N·m** stops slippage

### Uses
- Lengthening, bone transport into a defect, correction osteotomy
- Infected non-union, arthrodesis
- Clubfoot: the Ilizarov acts by **distraction histiogenesis** (Dr Mohamed Fathey)

- Bone transport frame after a segmental defect

### Distraction osteogenesis (Miller)
| Phase | Rule |
|---|---|
| **Latency** | **5–7 days** |
| **Distraction** | **1 mm/day**, in four steps |
| **Consolidation** | about twice the distraction time |

- Too slow, **0.5 mm/day** or less → premature consolidation (Rockwood)
- Too fast, **2 mm/day** or more → cysts, poor regenerate
- Keep the periosteum: low-energy corticotomy

#### How the bone forms
- Stable frame → bone forms directly (intramembranous), with no cartilage stage

#### Remove the frame
- Remove when **3 of 4** cortices of the regenerate are seen

- Rings only, before removal; regenerate healed on both views

### Osteogenesis or histiogenesis (Rockwood)
- **Osteogenesis**: new bone forms in the gap of a stretched bone
- **Histiogenesis**: slow tension also grows muscle, nerve, vessel and skin
- Bone responds best; nerves and vessels slowest

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Wait a week, a millimetre a day, consolidate twice as long**

PITFALL — "distract 2 mm a day to finish faster?"
- Fast distraction tears the new vessels; the gap fills with cysts
- Say → "**No. One millimetre a day, in four steps, after 5–7 days.**"

3.06.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what are these two frames?"
- "**Hybrid**: a ring with tensioned wires near the joint, half pins in the shaft."
- "**Hexapod**: two rings and **six struts**; a computer plans the correction."

### Hybrid fixator (AO)
- Usually **3/4** rings, with tensioned K-wires; Schanz screws in the shaft
- Used in proximal and distal tibial fractures: plateau and pilon

#### Make it stable (Rockwood)
- Periarticular ring: at least **three** tensioned wires
- Shaft: at least **four** half pins, more than one bar
- Two wires and far half pins → malunion or non-union

- Hybrid frame: AO drawing, and on a tibia
- Unstable hybrid: two distal wires, far shaft pins

PITFALL — "two wires on the hybrid ring are enough?"
- Two wires near a joint rarely cross at 90°, so the bone slides
- Say → "**No. At least three wires, and four shaft pins.**"

### Hexapod — Taylor Spatial Frame (TSF)
- A ring fixator with **6 struts** and **12 ball joints**
- Corrects **six axes** at once: angulation, translation, rotation, length

#### How it is used
- Software calculates each day's strut lengths
- Rings need not be parallel to the joints

#### Why it exists (Campbell)
- The Ilizarov frame corrects rotation poorly
- The hexapod needs precise measurements; an error changes the result

#### Acute use
- Wires, or at least **three** half pins each side

- Hexapod frames on the leg
- Tibial non-union corrected with a TSF

3.07.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "why a frame across this joint or pelvis?"
- "A **spanning frame** holds length until the soft tissues settle."
- "A **pelvic frame** closes the pelvic volume and helps control bleeding."

### Anterior pelvic frame (Campbell)
| Pin | Where | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Iliac crest** (gluteal pillar) | **2–4 cm** behind the ASIS | no fluoroscopy needed |
| **Supra-acetabular** | anterior inferior iliac spine | needs fluoroscopy; stronger |

- ASIS = anterior superior iliac spine
- Crest: two or three pins in each wing

#### Crest or supra-acetabular
- Crest pins loosen fast in cancellous bone
- Supra-acetabular pins grip the posterior column and spare the abdomen

#### When
- Best for rotationally unstable injuries: anteroposterior or lateral compression (Rockwood)
- Vertically unstable → add traction
- Anterior iliac wing or acetabular fracture → no pelvic frame

- Anterior iliac crest frame and its X-ray
- Supra-acetabular pins: fluoroscopy, X-ray, frame

### Knee-spanning frame (Harborview)
- For knee dislocation, distal femur and tibial plateau fractures
- Two **5 mm** pins in the femur, two in the tibia

#### Set-up
- Knee in **5–15°** of flexion
- Clamps away from the joint line; get computed tomography (CT) after the frame
- Over-distraction → compartment syndrome

- Knee-spanning frame; tibial plateau bridged on X-ray

### Ankle "delta" frame (AO)
- Two tibial pins and one calcaneal pin, joined in a triangle
- Add a **metatarsal pin** → no equinus
- Wait for the skin wrinkle sign, about **10 days**

#### Pins
- Calcaneal pin from medial, in the posteroinferior tuberosity
- Tibial pins anterior or medial; avoid lateral compartments

- Delta frame on a pilon fracture; reduced X-ray

PITFALL — "is one heel pin enough for a pilon frame?"
- The frame rotates about a single heel pin; the foot drops
- Say → "**Add a metatarsal pin: no rotation, no equinus.**"

3.07.2.b:
- For knee dislocation, distal femur and tibial plateau fractures
- Two **5 mm** pins in the femur, two in the tibia

#### Set-up
- Knee in **5–15°** of flexion
- Clamps away from the joint line; get computed tomography (CT) after the frame
- Over-distraction → compartment syndrome

- Knee-spanning frame; tibial plateau bridged on X-ray

3.07.3.b:
- Two tibial pins and one calcaneal pin, joined in a triangle
- Add a **metatarsal pin** → no equinus
- Wait for the skin wrinkle sign, about **10 days**

#### Pins
- Calcaneal pin from medial, in the posteroinferior tuberosity
- Tibial pins anterior or medial; avoid lateral compartments

- Delta frame on a pilon fracture; reduced X-ray

PITFALL — "is one heel pin enough for a pilon frame?"
- The frame rotates about a single heel pin; the foot drops
- Say → "**Add a metatarsal pin: no rotation, no equinus.**"

3.08.t: 3.8 What Goes Wrong and Pin-Site Care
3.08.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "complications of external fixation?"
- "**Pin-track infection** is the most common, then loosening and **ring sequestrum**."
- "Also nerve injury, joint stiffness, delayed union and malunion."

| Problem (Handbook; Campbell) | Note |
|---|---|
| **Pin-track infection** | most common |
| Loosening | follows heat and infection |
| **Ring sequestrum** | heat-killed ring of bone |
| Nerve, vessel injury | pin outside the safe zone |
| Joint stiffness | second most reported |
| Malunion, non-union | inadequate immobilisation |
| Refracture | through pin holes, after removal |

- Pin-track infection rate: up to **30%**
- Rigid spanning beyond **6–8 weeks** → joint ankylosis
- Ankle osteoarthritis follows tibial frames in **50–70%**

| Ankle osteoarthritis risk | Over |
|---|---|
| Age | **45** years |
| Body mass index | **25** |
| Time in the frame | **50 days** |

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Pus, loose, ring; nerve, stiff, malunion**

### Pin-track infection — Dahl grades (Rockwood)
| Grade | Finding | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| 0–1 | none or mild redness | pin care |
| 2–3 | serous or purulent discharge | oral antibiotics |
| 4 | lysis of both cortices | remove the pin |
| 5 | sequestrum, medullary abscess | surgical debridement |

- Pin-track infection with discharge around ring pins
- Pin sepsis on X-ray: sequestrum and cortical lucency

| Wrist-frame pins | Titanium | Steel |
|---|---|---|
| Removed early for infection | **0%** | **5%** |
| Loosening | **5%** | **10%** |

### Ring sequestrum (AO)
- Hot drilling kills a ring of cortex around the pin
- X-ray: sclerotic bone with a ring of lucency around it

#### Prevent
- Sharp drills, slow speed, predrilling, saline cooling
- Bone cells die above **50 °C**
- Predrilling lowers bone temperature by about **50%**

- Ring sequestrum after self-drilling pins

### Pin-site care (Nagah)
- Clean daily with saline or chlorhexidine; dry dressing
- Teach the patient the signs: redness, warmth, swelling, discharge

#### Rockwood adds
- Compressive dressings first → less skin motion at the pin
- No ointments; healed sites need only showering

- Compressive dressings around ring and foot pins

### Contraindications
- Extreme obesity that prevents safe pins
- Periprosthetic fracture with little bone stock
- A patient who refuses, cannot comply or cannot tolerate a frame

PITFALL — "a loose pin with discharge?"
- An infected pin has lost its hold; bone resorbs around it
- Say → "**Remove it and put a new pin at another site.**"
